Especially since at that age one sometimes sees it happen that the generative power begins to stir in the man, and the purgation of the flowers [the menses] in women <sup class="mk" data-key="t">t</sup>: and thus that the man and the woman can produce seed strong enough to conceive and beget <sup class="mk" data-key="u">u</sup>; although at the sixteenth year, and better still at the eighteenth, the natural power is far more robust and vigorous: whence our Jurisconsults have called the eighteenth year full and perfect puberty <sup class="mk" data-key="x">x</sup>, and have moreover taught that within the seventeenth year a man is still almost in his childhood <sup class="mk" data-key="y">y</sup>. Which the ancient Romans showed well in the children of Senators, or of other illustrious and honourable houses, whom until the seventeenth year they made wear the same fashion of clothing that they had worn in their first childhood, namely a long robe down to the heels, bordered all around with purple, which they called PRAETEXTA, with a small jewel of gold, in the shape of a heart, hung about their neck, which they called BULLA: so that, looking upon it, they might have occasion to think that they would not be esteemed men except insofar as their heart should be honest, good and virtuous <sup class="mk" data-key="z">z</sup>. And if anyone is still so curious as to wish to search out and understand the cause why women are sooner fit for marriage than men, I shall answer with Aristotle that, as females in their mother's womb, by reason of their coldness and weakness, are longer delayed in building and perfecting themselves, so as sometimes to wait until the tenth month — whereas the males, more vigorous and robust, scarcely pass the ninth — so also, when women are born, for the same reason of their feebleness and weakness, they grow and grow old sooner than males <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>. Whence this must be attributed to nature, which makes women sooner fit to beget, as being frailer, and sooner grown and aged <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>: after the example of every fruit, which, the smaller and slighter it is, ripens the more promptly and with the greater speed.

notes.citation: Digest 23.2.4 (De ritu nuptiarum, l. Minorem); Institutes 1.10 pr. (De nuptiis); Decretals, X 4.2 (De desponsatione impuberum), c. Puberes
notes.original: L. minorem D. de rit. nup paragr. i. de nu, aux Inſtitutions de Iuſtinien c. pube res. de deſponſ. impub.
notes.gloss: Institutes: lawful marriage is contracted by males who are puberes and females who are viripotentes; the "paragr. i." may be the principium or § 1.

notes.citation: Aristotle, History of Animals V.14 (544b), cf. VII.1 (581a)
notes.original: Ariſtote au v. de la nature des animaux x. c. v.
notes.gloss: Coras's reference is garbled ("au v. ... x. c. v."); both passages put the first production of seed in males and the first menses in females at about fourteen.

notes.citation: Macrobius, Commentary on the Dream of Scipio I.6 (§§ 70–71)
notes.original: Macrobe au ſonge de Scipion c. vi.
notes.gloss: On the number seven: at twice seven years the generative power appears in males and the menses in females.

notes.citation: Digest 1.7 (De adoptionibus et emancipationibus), l. Arrogato § 1, fragment not identified; Digest 34.1.14 (De alimentis vel cibariis legatis, l. Mela) § 1
notes.original: L. arrogato. paragr. i. D. de adoptio I, Mela para. i. De ali. leg
notes.gloss: Ulpian reporting Mela: in legacies of maintenance "full puberty" is taken to be eighteen years.

notes.original: L. i. parag. pueritiam. D. de poſtul.
notes.gloss: Ulpian: the praetor forbids one under seventeen to plead before him, "because he judged this age to be moderate."

notes.original: Macrobe au premier liure des Saturnales. c. vi.
notes.gloss: The origin of the praetexta and of the heart-shaped bulla worn by boys of senatorial families, and its moral meaning.

notes.citation: Aristotle, Generation of Animals IV.6 (775a) and cf. IV.7; History of Animals VII.4 (cf. VII.3, 583b–584b)
notes.original: Ariſtote au iiij, de la generation des animaux c. vi, & vij. & au liure de la nature d'iceux. cap. iiij.
notes.gloss: Females, being colder and weaker, are formed more slowly in the womb but after birth reach maturity and old age sooner than males. The History of Animals book number is not given by Coras.

notes.citation: Pliny, Natural History VII.3 in the old chapter division (cf. modern VII.4–6, on gestation and the formation of the sexes)
notes.original: Pline au vij liure de la naturelle hiſtoire. c. iij.
